To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mu opioid receptors are located in the medullary neurons that are the source for parasympathetically innervated organs, and the expression of these receptors is reduced by vagotomy.

mu opioid receptors, which are expressed in preganglionic neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), are transported to their peripheral targets in the gastrointestinal tract, and that vagotomy leads to depletion of mu opioid receptors in NTS.
mu opioid receptors, the most abundant opioid receptor type in the brain, are expressed in preganglionic neurons that control the parasympathic nervous system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the expression of the mu opioid receptor mRNA in preganglionic neurons of the medulla oblongata.
the identification of the neuronal source of the mu opioid receptor acting on the vagus nerve.
the identification and characterization of opioid receptors in the brain and the spinal cord.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vagal preganglionic neurons express mu opioid receptors, which can be axonally transported and which are involved in vagal reflexes, and which may be the site for opioid action.
the vagal preganglionic neurons in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV) and the nucleus ambiguous (NA) are the source for the mu opioid receptors in the vagal parasymparthetic outflow.
mu opioid receptors are expressed in preganglionic parasympathetics, which are involved in cardiorespirational regulation, and in the vagal afferents, which mediate the effects of vagotomy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mu opioid receptor mRNA in the medullary vagal preganglionic neurons is synthesized in the cell body and is transported to the periphery where it is inserted into the plasma membranes of the vagal terminals.

the medullally projecting vagal preganglionic neurons, the major source of vagal outflow, express mu opioid receptor mRNA, and that the mRNA is transported to the terminals of the axon and is depleted following vagotomy.

mu opioid receptor mRNA in the medullary pre- ganglionic neurons is transported distally to the target organs, and that the mRNA is translated to functional receptors in the target organs, where they act as autoregulatory receptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the opioid receptor is expressed by the preganglionic neurons in the medulla and that these neurons can be targeted to reduce the risk of opioid overdose.
vagal afferent activity is not required to maintain the expression of the mu opioid receptors in the nucleus of the solitary tract.
we have a new way to look at the opioid system in a very specific way.
